newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Govt troops move into abandoned Tajik valley.
newsitem.headline: Govt troops move into abandoned Tajik valley.

text.p: Shell casings and spent rockets littered the road through scorched fields in Tajikistan's Fakhrobad valley on Wednesday after a rebel colonel abandoned his positions.

The government said mutinous Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev had agreed to withdraw his troops from the valley, about 25 km (15 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe, and give up command of his elite armoured brigade.
He had fought troops loyal to embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov since Saturday.
"Khudoyberdyev has resigned as commander of his brigade and will work in another post," said Rakhmonov's spokesman, Zafar Saidov.
"Capitulation," was how tired government troops strung out along the road described it.
"They left this morning, it's all quiet now," said a pro-government commander wearing belts of ammunition and a black baseball cap emblazoned with a skull and crossbones.
Stationed at a lonely post on the road in the treeless, empty valley, he and his men look tired but relieved that the fighting was over. Blank-faced, they munched on grapes.

A jeep mounted with a heavy machinegun shuddered to a halt. A soldier stood up inside and whooped as he fired off a clip of ammunition from an assault rifle in celebration, the empty cartidges bouncing on the tarmac.
The road south had been officially reopened but the occasional battered old Lada car full of fighters bristling with guns formed the only traffic.
The burnt carcasses of three cars, destroyed by rocket fire, lay in a bend in the road nearby.
It appeared to be third time unlucky for Khudoyberdyev, 34, politically ambitious and who in two previous mutinies won major concessions from Rakhmonov's shaky administration.
Khudoyberdyev lost part of his booty, an aluminium smelter west of the capital, to pro-government forces on Monday.
The colonel had also sniped at a peace deal to end four years of bloody civil war which Rakhmonov signed in June with the republic's armed Islamic opposition.
Khudoyberdyev said the imminent return of Islamist fighters to Dushanbe would provoke more bloodshed.

But it was weekend clashes in Dushanbe between rival warlords -- both nominally loyal to the government -- and the ensuing fighting with Khudoyberdyev after he moved armour towards the capital which threatened the chronically unstable former Soviet republic with a return to civil war.
"We're not celebrating victory," said one soldier at the post, his eyes screwed up in the hot afternoon sun. "We're celebrating peace".
